articles.text: We had to tread around on the pedal extremities of the Black Hills Pioneer quite a while before we found the sore spot, but we finally struck it. articles.text: The con's and their ladies took the town of Medora by storm last week. Made a raid on the news depot, and played smash generally. They visited the slaughter-house under the guidance of the Marquis and his employes detailed for that purpose, and were unanimous in their expressions of admiration of the perfection of all the arrangements. They will probably stop on their return and see the business when it is under full headway. They were a fine looking body of men—the ladies were—well, we are not very well up in that line, but langnage fails to express etc.
articles.summary: Visiting 'con's' and their ladies toured Medora last week, including the Marquis' slaughter-house.

articles.text: "What benefit is the Montana Stockmens association to us"? This is the question which the Dakota stockmen are asking, and no one seems to be able to answer. They say, "we have paid our money whenever it has been asked for, and in return supposed we would be entitled to some of the benefits of the association. Late developments would seem to indicate that such are not the views of the association. We think it important and that not only Dakota interests but those of eastern Montana, demand that we should have a stock inspector located at Medora. We are told by the association that they 'can not furnish one because all the inspectors are employed and paid by the Board of stock commissioners and are Territorial officers, and the funds to pay them are raised by taxation, which is paid to the county Treasurers, who in turn pay the inspectors.' It seems a little strange that no arrangement has been made for emergencies of this kind." It will be remembered that the BAD LANDS COW BOY, from the start advocated that it would be better to have an association of our own here in Dakota, but it was thought at the time by the stockmen that the expenses of a separate association would be greater than the benefits we were likely to receive. It now looks as if we were likely to pay two expenses for one benefit, as the Montana association says that if there is an inspector here the stockmen must pay for it themselves. It is to be hoped that the Montana association will reconsider the matter and do the fair thing by us.
articles.summary: Editorial complaining that the Montana Stockmen's association will not furnish a stock inspector at Medora.

articles.text: The Miles City Stock Grower commenting on the difference of opinion prevailing among cattlemen in regard to some of the more important questions of the cattle business, says, "one man will tell you to stock your range with Short-horns, another will insist upon Herefords, and so on through all the different breeds of cattle. Some will tell you to let bulls run on the range all the time, and others will tell you to take up your bulls in the fall without fail, and still others will tell me that I am an idiot to think of putting anything on my range but steers." In replying to this we would say that without doubt there are a great many theoretical stockmen even in the same section of country, with widely different opinions, on such questions. The practical men are those who are constantly on the range and know from experience. It is also true that a class of cattle suitable to a range in Montana, might be entirely unsuitable to a range in Texas, and in southern countries it might be more profitable to let the bulls run the year round, while in northern countries the bulls should be rounded up in the fall. There can be no invariable rule established, by which the stock business can be run. Common sense, with a "right smart" stock of practical experience, together with a knowledge of the climate and seasons of the country in which the location is to be made, are the principal requisites of succesful investment in the cattle business. If the capitalist is not personally in posession of these essentials, and is not willing to pay an exorbitant price for experience, our advice would be to first engage a man who has, and then leave the management of affairs to him. Men do this in other classes of business, and why should they not in this. If the capitalist will put himself under the tuition of a good competent foreman on his own range, he can learn the business at his leisure, and to much better effect than to go about asking opinions of theoretical cranks.
articles.summary: Editorial reply to the Miles City Stock Grower on practical versus theoretical stockmen.

articles.text: It is rapidly becoming an established fact that the valley of the Little Missouri river will in the near future be noted for its fine horses. The grasses are richer and more nourishing than even the famous blue grass of Kentucky. The soil is hard and dry and nowhere can horses be found with better feet. Pure spring water is abundant, and the rarity of the atmosphere is just sufficient to insure good wind. The two minute horse will come from the northwest.
articles.summary: Paragraph promoting the Little Missouri valley as horse-raising country.

articles.text: EDITORS BAD LANDS COW BOY:—As the quarantine subject has become a question of grave importance I would like to express my views through the columns of your valuable paper. I have tried to keep myself posted, and from the different stock Journals I obtain my information. It appears that pleuro-pneumonia is dying out and now the veterinarians are more seriously affected than the cattle have been. Stock Journals disclaim the existence of pleuro-pneumonia and veterinarians insist on strict quarantine, if not for one reason, for another, as will be seen in the case of T. Corwin Anderson a breeder of blooded stock in Kentucky. After his public sale of bulls he was approached by the state veterinarian for the state of Illinois who tried to impress upon Mr. Anderson's mind that it was absolutely necessary for him to secure his (Dr. Paaren's) certificate of health before shipping his bulls to the purchasers, and intimated that his services were worth $5,00 per head of cattle inspected, but subsequently reduced the price to $20,00 for the lot, stating that if they were all together the inspection would not take long. If I have been rightly informed it is undoubtedly his duty to inspect those cattle and is paid for his services by the state at the rate of $8,00 per diem. It is simply a scheme gotten up to employ a few men who are willing to resort to such means to extort money from the cattleman. According to the statement made by the National Live Stock Journal, Mr. Anderson had paid all expenses in his own state, of strict compliance with all that the laws of any other state requires, and it should not be required of him to pay extra. What is needed on the ranges of the west is more bulls, and if cattlemen can not get their bulls from the east without havinS them held and inspected at an additional expense of about $5,00 per head for every health certificate issued by the different veterinarians of states through which they have to pass, they will have to resort to some other source for their blooded stock.—[Cow-Puncher.
articles.summary: Letter (credited to the Cow-Puncher) attacking veterinary quarantine fees on blooded bulls.

articles.text: The horse industry of this Territory is yet in its infancy, but is rapidly coming to the front and in a few years at most Montana horseflesh will prove a formidable rival to America's favorite Kentucky horses. An exchange says: "It requires three or four years to convince the cattle-growers of Montana that their beef products could be marketed in the east, but the horsemen will not be slow in being brought to realize this fact. It has now been scarcely twelve months since the first carload of horses went forward, but we find that there has already been more horses forwarded this way east than there were cattle for the first two years. Already it may be said, the industry is fully established and that there need in the future be no more surplus of horses in Montana. It is, indeed, remarkable how soon the tables turn. Only a few years ago a few expert drovers were just coining money shipping in state,s horses (geldings), which found a ready sale. Now our territory has not only become self-supporting, but has horses to sell. It is true we are still receiving large consignments of stallions and mares for breeding purposes and will continue to for some time yet to come, but we are in a position to grow work horses cheaper than any other portion of America and the superiority of the animals grown over that of other sctions is a sure guarantee of a steady and reliable market.—[Glendive Independnet.
articles.summary: Clipping from the Glendive Independent on the growth of the Montana horse industry.

articles.headline: THE LOST CABIN GOLD MINES.
articles.text:
THE LOST CABIN GOLD MINES.

By J. S. WARN.

Many conjectures and newspaper reports have been scattered broadcast over the country from time to time, in regard to the Lost Cabin mines of the Big Horn mountains. My friends have many times requested me to write the history of the mines, as my uncle, Allen Hulburt, the original discoverer, told it to me. As will be seen later on, I went on the first expedition with my uncle after he was driven out by the Indians.

In the spring of 1849 Allen Hulburt of Jonesville, Wis., in company with others started overland for the gold mines of California. They arrived there in October of the same year, having endured many hardships and perils in their five months trip across the plains. Years passed, and his family and friends received no word from him, and after diligent inquiry, could not learn of his whereabouts and concluded that he must have perished on the plains. In this however they were mistaken, for all these years he was in the mountains prospecting and mining, always confident, as only miners can appreciate, that the next day might open a "rich find" and he would be able to return to his family and friends with untold wealth at his command. Thus time rolled on until the spring of 1863, when he in company with Wm. Jones and Jos. Cox, left California and went to Walla Walla, Washington Ter. Arriving there they bought an outfit of six horses and the other necessaries for prospecting east of the Rocky Mountains. Leaving Walla Walla, they took the old Mullen trail for the eastern side, prospecting as they went, whenever there were any signs of colors. The Indians were always on their trail and never failed to give them trouble when opportunity offered. Undaunted by the perils surrounding them they still moved on, sometimes by night and sometimes by day, until they finally reached the valley of the Yellowstone, which they struck below the mouth of the Big Horn river.

It has been generally believed that they had crossed the Big Horn river previous to this time, but I will endeavor to show that such was not the case, and also that they never got into the Big Horn mountains to prospect, as Mr. Hulburt supposed at the time. It was very easy to be mistaken in those days, when the geography of that country was so little known. He says that where the mines were, there was no snow until November, and it is a well known fact that there is snow in the Big Horn mountains the year round. I have been there at all seasons of the year and know whereof I speak.

When the party struck the Yellowstone they crossed a branch of it on to an island and went into camp to give themselves and their stock a chance to recruit up and to reconoitre and find where to get out of the valley and avoid the Indians. After resting two days they made up their minds as to the best route, and at dark struck out, crossing the other branch of the river and arrived safely on the southern bank. Proceeding southward they left the valley and travelled over a rolling prairie until daylight when they went into camp. Just ahead of them could be seen a range of mountains. That night they started again and at daylight were in sight of a stream that was undoubtedly the Rosebud.

(to be continued.)
articles.summary: First installment of J. S. Warn's history of the Lost Cabin gold mines and his uncle Allen Hulburt's 1863 expedition.

articles.text: Dr. H. M. Jorgens returned to Medora Wednesday, having spent the last four weeks in the Hills.

articles.text: Mr. Gordon, the genial proprietor of the clothing store and one of the rustlers of the COW BOY took dinner with Tom Martin up at Sully creek last Sunday. Tom knows what the boys need about three times a day. The "Kid" is a pretty good hand at "stowing away ballast" too and don't you let that escape from the tablets of your memory.
articles.summary: Mr. Gordon of the clothing store dined with Tom Martin at Sully creek last Sunday.

articles.text: Some folks will rope a Texas steer when they get a chance and then again some wont. Ask that cowboy who was riding a gray horse the other evening why he did n't show his dexterity, and he will find more excuses for you than he would if he was on trial for his sins.
articles.summary: Joke about a cowboy who failed to rope a Texas steer.

articles.text: Miss Janie F. Hayford, class of '84 O. C., daughter of Mr. and Mrs. W. H. Hayford of No. 13 Forest street, was married on wednesday evening of this week to Mr. A. T. Packard, who studied some time in Oberlin and graduated at Ann Arbor, Prof. J. M. Ellis officiating. Mr. Packard is now an enterprising newspaper man of Medora, Dakota, his paper bearing the unique title of "The Bad Lands Cow Boy."—[Oberlin Weekly News.
articles.summary: Reprinted Oberlin notice of A. T. Packard's marriage to Miss Janie F. Hayford.

articles.text: A letter received from A. T. Packard this week says, "we will leave LaPorte for Chicago Wednesday, remain there about a week and then start for Medora." Judging from the plural pronoun and the marriage notice, clipped from an Oberlin paper, which we take the liberty to publish, we are led to conclude that congratulations are in order.
articles.summary: Packard writes that he and his bride will leave LaPorte for Chicago Wednesday and then come to Medora.

articles.text: A real, "live cowboy" was a greater object of wonder and admiration to the Con's and their ladies than anything else in Medora. John Goodall, the Marquis' foreman, was the victim. He had both arms and one leg talked loose, was "held up" for all the cartridges in his belt, and presented a generally dilapidated appearance when he emerged from the car where one of the Con's had invited him to sample some patent lemonade.
articles.summary: The visiting 'Con's' made a curiosity of John Goodall, the Marquis' foreman.

articles.text: Slaughtering began at the abbatoirs here Tuesday June 2nd. Seventy cattle were killed. They dressed out very well for the early season. The working at the abbatoirs is in fine systematic shape, and everything seems to fit in its place like a set of cog-wheels. Mr. Foster, the superintendent, appears to know what is needed and how to use it. We cannot but congratulate the Marquis on securing the services of so valuable an assistant, and the people of Medora, on the additional assurance this gives of the ultimate success of the business which insures our prosperity as a town.
articles.summary: Slaughtering began at the Medora abattoir on Tuesday, June 2, with seventy cattle killed.

articles.text: Mr. Martin has received a full supply of blanks and instructions from the weather bureau for making weather reports. What is needed now is a supply of instruments for making correct observations. These reports are published weekly in the COW BOY by special request of some of our stockmen. Will they not use their influence with the weather bureau to secure Mr. Martin a set of the necessary instruments free of charge. We can also probably secure daily telegraph weather reports, which may at times be of considerable value to us.
articles.summary: T. Martin received weather-bureau blanks; the paper asks stockmen to help get him instruments.

articles.text:
Marquis de Mores has this week sent out hand bills offering a reward of $20. per head for four horses estrayed from Gallups ranch near Cave Hills, and two horses estrayed from Medora. It is believed that the two Medora horses have been stolen and $500. reward is offered for the thief or thieves delivered at Medora. This is a move in the right direction, and much to be commended. It is in our opinion far better than the "strangling" committee sent out by the Montana outfits sometime since

[Later. The two horses strayed from Medora have been found, but the other four are still at large.]
articles.summary: The Marquis offered rewards for six strayed horses and $500 for any thief; the two Medora horses were later found.
